title: Direct Methods for Visual SLAM
blurb: Why feature-based pipelines throw information away, how direct image alignment optimises the photometric error instead, the structure of its Jacobian and the inverse-compositional trick, and how pose-graph optimisation with loop closure keeps a large-scale map globally consistent.

knowledge_points.title: Feature-Based versus Direct Methods
knowledge_points.recap:
**Shortcomings of the classical (feature-based) pipeline.** Detect keypoints → describe → match → estimate geometry → bundle-adjust. All the photometric information in the image is compressed into a few hundred points, so: the reconstruction is **sparse**; performance collapses in **low-texture** scenes where few corners exist; matching errors (outliers) must be handled explicitly by RANSAC; and the intermediate abstraction discards precisely the intensity data that carries fine geometry.
**Direct methods.** Skip the feature layer entirely and optimise pose (and optionally depth) so that the **image intensities themselves** agree. The residual is photometric,
$$r_i(\xi)=I_2\big(\tau(\xi,x_i)\big)-I_1(x_i),$$
where $\tau$ warps a pixel of image 1 into image 2 given the pose $\xi\in\mathfrak{se}(3)$ and the pixel's depth. Bundle adjustment minimises a **geometric** error; direct alignment a **photometric** one; the eight-point algorithm neither.
**Unknowns.** In direct methods the unknowns are the camera **poses** (and optionally depth maps) with **all** pixels contributing; in feature-based methods the unknowns are poses **and** the 3D coordinates of the matched landmarks, with only those points contributing.
**Advantages of direct methods.** Use all (or semi-dense) image information ⇒ **dense / semi-dense** reconstruction; work where there are no corners but there is a gradient (edges, faint texture); no feature-matching outliers; higher accuracy at the sub-pixel level.
**Disadvantages.** Rely on **brightness constancy**, so they break under illumination change, auto-exposure, specularities and rolling shutter unless a photometric model is added; the photometric cost is highly **non-convex**, so a good initialisation and a coarse-to-fine pyramid are essential; and they are computationally heavier per frame.
**From brightness to irradiance constancy.** DSO replaces brightness constancy with an explicit **photometric camera model** (exposure time, vignetting, response function), i.e. **irradiance** constancy — which is what makes a direct method usable on real, auto-exposed video.
**2023 paper focus.** Direct methods do not first extract and match features. Semi-dense methods select high-gradient pixels, sparse direct methods still minimise intensity residuals, and processing more pixels generally makes dense methods slower.

questions.q: (a) In direct methods the unknowns are camera poses (and optionally depth maps); what are they in feature-based methods? (b) Direct methods assume brightness constancy — name two advantages and two disadvantages.
questions.answer:
**(a)** In feature-based (indirect) methods the unknowns are the camera **poses together with the 3D coordinates of the matched landmarks**. Only the extracted keypoints enter the cost; the rest of the image is discarded. Direct methods instead keep every pixel (or a semi-dense subset) and parameterise geometry by per-pixel **depth**.
**(b) Advantages.** (1) They exploit **all** the image information, so they can operate on edges and faint gradients where no corner detector fires, and they yield a **dense or semi-dense** reconstruction. (2) There is no feature-matching stage, hence no matching outliers to reject, and the sub-pixel accuracy is typically higher.
**Disadvantages.** (1) Brightness constancy is fragile: illumination change, auto-exposure, vignetting, specular highlights and rolling shutter all violate it, so a photometric camera model must be calibrated and estimated. (2) The photometric cost is strongly **non-convex** with a small basin of convergence, so a good initialisation and coarse-to-fine optimisation are mandatory, and the per-frame cost is higher.
questions.extend: DSO's answer to disadvantage (1) is to model exposure, vignetting and response explicitly — replacing brightness constancy with **irradiance** constancy.

questions.q: What are the shortcomings of classical (feature-based) approaches to multiple-view reconstruction that motivate direct methods?
questions.answer:
**Information is thrown away.** The pipeline reduces a full image to a few hundred keypoints and descriptors; everything else — edges, faint texture, the intensity profile itself — is discarded before any geometry is estimated.
**Sparse output.** The reconstruction consists only of the matched landmarks, so a dense surface has to be recovered afterwards by a separate multi-view stereo stage.
**Fails in low-texture scenes.** Corner detectors need two dominant gradient directions; on white walls, sky or repetitive structures there simply are not enough reliable keypoints.
**Matching outliers.** Descriptor matching produces wrong correspondences that must be removed by RANSAC, and its assumptions can fail with repetitive structure.
**Cascaded errors.** Each stage (detection, description, matching, geometry) commits to a hard decision, and an early mistake cannot be repaired later.
**Direct methods** address all of these by optimising pose and depth directly against the image intensities, keeping the full photometric information in the loop.

questions.q: A direct tracker augments brightness constancy with $I_2(\tau(\xi,x_i))\approx aI_1(x_i)+b$. Write the residual and its Jacobian blocks with respect to the pose increment $\xi$, gain $a$, and bias $b$. Which illumination changes can this model absorb, and which cannot it repair?
questions.answer:
Use
$$r_i(\xi,a,b)=I_2(\tau(\xi,x_i))-aI_1(x_i)-b.$$
At the current estimate,
$$\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial\xi}=\nabla I_2\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial X}\frac{\partial(Tp_i)}{\partial\xi},\qquad \frac{\partial r_i}{\partial a}=-I_1(x_i),\qquad \frac{\partial r_i}{\partial b}=-1.$$
A global exposure/gain and offset can be modeled. Spatially varying shadows, specularities, saturation, motion blur, and occlusion are not one global affine change; robust weights or a richer photometric model are still needed.
questions.extend: Cremers-style coverage question; not a past-paper citation.

questions.q: Choose between a feature-based, a direct, or a hybrid visual-odometry front end for each case: (i) a weakly textured wall with faint gradients, (ii) a large viewpoint jump, and (iii) auto-exposed video with repeated texture. Justify each choice in terms of information used, convergence basin, and outlier handling.
questions.answer: **(i)** A direct or semi-direct method can use the faint gradients even when no repeatable corners exist. **(ii)** Descriptor-based features have a larger discrete matching basin than local photometric optimization and are the safer initializer. **(iii)** A hybrid is appropriate: invariant or learned matches plus geometric RANSAC handle repeated texture and large association errors, while a calibrated photometric model and direct refinement recover sub-pixel accuracy. Direct methods avoid feature-matching outliers but have a narrow, non-convex basin; feature methods discard dense intensity information but tolerate larger displacement.
questions.extend: Cremers-style coverage question; not a past-paper citation.

questions.q: Which statements about direct SLAM methods are **wrong**?
questions.answer: **Wrong: 1, 2 and 4.** Direct methods optimise image intensities without a separate feature-tracking stage. Semi-dense methods select high-gradient pixels. Dense methods are normally slower because they use more pixels. Sparse direct methods still minimise photometric residuals and are not equivalent to feature-based systems such as ORB-SLAM.

options.text: A direct SLAM method first tracks features and then determines camera motion from them.
A semi-dense direct method typically tracks pixels with small gradients.
A dense direct method is typically slower than semi-dense and sparse direct methods.
A sparse direct method is equivalent to a feature-based method such as ORB-SLAM.

knowledge_points.title: Direct Image Alignment: Residual, Jacobian and Inverse Composition
knowledge_points.recap:
**Residual.** For a pixel $x_i$ with known depth, warped by a pose increment $\xi\in\mathfrak{se}(3)$,
$$r_i(\xi)=I_2\big(\tau(\xi,x_i)\big)-I_1(x_i),\qquad \tau(\xi,x)=\pi\big(T(\xi)\,p(x)\big),$$
where $p(x)$ back-projects the pixel to 3D and $\pi$ projects it back. At zero motion the warp is the identity, $\tau(0,x)=x$, so $r_i(0)=I_2(x_i)-I_1(x_i)$ — the raw intensity difference.
**Why the pose cannot be optimised over $SE(3)$ directly.** $SE(3)$ is a manifold, not a vector space, so one optimises the **twist increment** $\xi\in\mathfrak{se}(3)\cong\mathbb{R}^6$ and updates by left multiplication $T\leftarrow\exp(\hat\xi)T$ — six unconstrained parameters instead of a constrained $4\times4$ matrix.
**Jacobian by the chain rule — three factors:**
$$J_i=\underbrace{\nabla I_2}_{1\times2}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial X}}_{2\times3}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\partial\big(T(\xi)p\big)}{\partial\xi}}_{3\times6}\ \in\mathbb{R}^{1\times6}.$$
(1) the **image gradient** of the second image at the warped location; (2) the Jacobian of the **projection**, which for $\pi(X,Y,Z)=\big(f_x\tfrac XZ+c_x,\ f_y\tfrac YZ+c_y\big)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}f_x/Z&0&-f_xX/Z^2\\0&f_y/Z&-f_yY/Z^2\end{pmatrix}$; (3) the Jacobian of the **$SE(3)$ action** on the 3D point, evaluated at $\xi=0$, which is $\big(I_{3\times3}\ \ -\hat p\big)$.
**Gauss–Newton system.** $(J^\top J)\Delta\xi=-J^\top r$ with $J\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times6}$, so $J^\top J\in\mathbb{R}^{6\times6}$ **regardless of the number of pixels** $N$ — and it accumulates as $J^\top J=\sum_{i=1}^{N}J_i^\top J_i$, one rank-1 update per pixel. Memory is $O(1)$, not $O(N)$: never form $J$ explicitly.
**Inverse compositional formulation.** Swap which image is warped: $r_i(\Delta\xi)=I_1\big(\tau(\Delta\xi,x_i)\big)-I_2\big(\tau(\xi,x_i)\big)$. Now the Jacobian depends only on $I_1$ and the **reference** geometry, both of which are fixed, so $J$ **and $J^\top J$ can be precomputed once** before the iteration; only the residual is re-evaluated each step. The saving is large: the expensive gradient/Jacobian computation and the $6\times6$ accumulation move out of the loop, leaving only a warp and an image lookup per iteration.
**Coarse-to-fine.** The linearisation is valid only locally, so alignment runs on an image pyramid exactly as in Lucas–Kanade — coarse levels capture large motion, fine levels refine it.
**2023 paper focus.** Direct warping follows $p\mapsto K(R(dK^{-1}p)+t)$ and is non-convex, so initialisation matters. Robust kernels suppress bad residuals. Photometric calibration corrects response, exposure and vignetting; rolling shutter is a geometric timing effect.

questions.q: For the photometric residual $r_i(\xi)=I_2(\tau(\xi,x_i))-I_1(x_i)$: (a) what is $\tau(0,x)$ and what is $r_i(0)$? (b) Why can't we optimise directly over the elements of $SE(3)$?
questions.answer:
**(a)** $\tau(0,x)=x$ — warping with zero motion is the identity, since $T(0)=\exp(\hat0)=I$. Hence
$$r_i(0)=I_2(x_i)-I_1(x_i),$$
the plain intensity difference at the same pixel.
**(b)** $SE(3)$ is a **curved manifold**, not a vector space: its elements are $4\times4$ matrices subject to $R^\top R=I$, $\det R=1$ and the fixed bottom row. A Gauss–Newton step adds an unconstrained increment, which would immediately leave the manifold. Instead one optimises over the **Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{se}(3)\cong\mathbb{R}^6$ — six unconstrained twist coordinates — and applies the update multiplicatively, $T\leftarrow\exp(\widehat{\Delta\xi})\,T$, which stays in $SE(3)$ by construction.
questions.extend: Same pattern as Chapter 2: a manifold-valued unknown is optimised through a local chart given by the exponential map.

questions.q: (a) Apply the chain rule to decompose the Jacobian $J_i$ of the photometric residual into three factors and identify them. (b) For $\pi(X,Y,Z)=(f_xX/Z+c_x,\ f_yY/Z+c_y)$, compute the projection Jacobian. (c) What is the Jacobian of the $SE(3)$ action on a 3D point at $\xi=0$? (d) Why is coarse-to-fine optimisation needed?
questions.answer:
**(a)** $$J_i=\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial\xi}=\underbrace{\nabla I_2\big(\tau(\xi,x_i)\big)}_{1\times2:\ \text{image gradient}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial X}}_{2\times3:\ \text{projection}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\partial\big(T(\xi)p\big)}{\partial\xi}}_{3\times6:\ SE(3)\ \text{action}}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times6}.$$
**(b)** By the quotient rule,
$$\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial(X,Y,Z)}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{f_x}{Z}&0&-\dfrac{f_xX}{Z^2}\\[2mm]0&\dfrac{f_y}{Z}&-\dfrac{f_yY}{Z^2}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times3}.$$
**(c)** With $T(\xi)p\approx p+\xi_v+\omega\times p$ for small $\xi=(\xi_v,\omega)$,
$$\frac{\partial\big(T(\xi)p\big)}{\partial\xi}\bigg|_{\xi=0}=\big(I_{3\times3}\ \ \ -\hat p\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times6},$$
since $\omega\times p=-p\times\omega=-\hat p\,\omega$.
**(d)** The residual is linearised around the current pose, and image intensities vary on the scale of a pixel — so the approximation is valid only for **small** motions. For larger motions one aligns on an **image pyramid**, coarse levels first (where the motion is a fraction of a pixel), passing each estimate down to initialise the next finer level.
questions.extend: The $1/Z$ and $1/Z^2$ factors mean far-away points contribute almost nothing to the pose Jacobian — direct methods are driven by nearby, high-gradient pixels.

questions.q: (a) Write the Jacobian of the inverse-compositional residual $r_i(\Delta\xi)=I_1(\tau(\Delta\xi,x_i))-I_2(\tau(\xi,x_i))$ with respect to $\Delta\xi$. (b) Why can this Jacobian be precomputed once before the iteration starts, and what changes each iteration? (c) What is the computational saving compared with the forward formulation?
questions.answer:
**(a)** Only the **first** term depends on $\Delta\xi$, so by the same chain rule evaluated at $\Delta\xi=0$:
$$J_i=\nabla I_1(x_i)\cdot\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial X}\cdot\big(I_{3\times3}\ \ -\hat p_i\big).$$
**(b)** Every factor depends only on the **reference** image $I_1$ and the reference geometry (the back-projected point $p_i$ at its known depth) — none of them depends on the current pose estimate $\xi$. They are therefore constant throughout the optimisation and can be computed **once**, together with $J^\top J$ and its factorisation. What changes each iteration is only the **residual**: the second image must be re-warped with the current $\xi$ and subtracted.
**(c)** The expensive per-pixel work — image-gradient lookup, the two Jacobian multiplications and the accumulation of the $6\times6$ matrix $J^\top J=\sum_iJ_i^\top J_i$ (plus its Cholesky factorisation) — moves **out of the loop**. Each iteration then costs one warp, one image lookup per pixel and a $6$-vector accumulation for $J^\top r$, followed by a back-substitution. For a semi-dense pixel set that is a large constant-factor speed-up, which is what makes real-time direct SLAM feasible.
questions.extend: The price is that the increment composes on the *other* side: the update is $T\leftarrow T\,\exp(\widehat{\Delta\xi})^{-1}$ rather than a plain left multiplication.

questions.q: The Gauss–Newton system for direct image alignment is $(J^\top J)\Delta\xi=-J^\top r$. (a) What are the dimensions of $J^\top J$ and $J^\top r$ for $N$ pixels? (b) Show that $J^\top J=\sum_{i=1}^{N}J_i^\top J_i$ and explain the memory consequence.
questions.answer:
**(a)** Each pixel contributes one scalar residual and a $1\times6$ Jacobian row, so $J\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times6}$ and $r\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Therefore
$$J^\top J\in\mathbb{R}^{6\times6},\qquad J^\top r\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$$
— **independent of the number of pixels $N$**.
**(b)** Writing $J$ row-wise as $J=(J_1^\top,\dots,J_N^\top)^\top$ with $J_i\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times6}$,
$$J^\top J=\sum_{i=1}^{N}J_i^\top J_i,\qquad J^\top r=\sum_{i=1}^{N}J_i^\top r_i.$$
**Memory consequence.** The full $N\times6$ Jacobian never has to be stored: one iterates over pixels, accumulating a $6\times6$ matrix and a $6$-vector. Memory is $O(1)$ in the number of pixels (and the accumulation parallelises trivially over pixels), which is exactly why a direct method can use hundreds of thousands of pixels in real time.
questions.extend: The same rank-1 accumulation pattern appears in the structure tensor of Lucas–Kanade — it is the standard way to build normal equations without materialising $J$.

questions.q: An RGB-D tracker aligns a live frame to a reference frame. Let $p_i$ be a reference 3D point, $q_i$ the corresponding live-frame 3D point, $n_i$ the live surface normal, and $T(\xi)$ the candidate pose. (a) Write a point-to-plane geometric residual and a photometric residual. (b) Give a combined energy. (c) Why are the two residuals complementary?
questions.answer:
**Residuals.** A point-to-plane ICP residual is
$$r_i^g(\xi)=n_i^\top\big(T(\xi)p_i-q_i\big),$$
while the direct photometric residual is
$$r_i^I(\xi)=I_2\big(\pi(T(\xi)p_i)\big)-I_1\big(\pi(p_i)\big).$$
A combined robust least-squares objective is, for example,
$$E(\xi)=\sum_i w_i^g\,\rho\big((r_i^g)^2\big)+\lambda\sum_i w_i^I\,\rho\big((r_i^I)^2\big).$$
**Complementarity.** The geometric term uses measured depth and surface normals, so it remains informative on textureless surfaces where the image gradient is zero. The photometric term supplies sub-pixel constraints from texture and can constrain directions to which a locally planar point-to-plane residual is weak. Combining them improves conditioning and robustness, provided invalid depths, occlusions and illumination changes are down-weighted.
questions.extend: Point-to-plane ICP measures only the displacement along the normal; tangential motion on a flat surface needs texture or additional geometry to become observable.

questions.q: In direct image alignment the approximate Hessian is $H=\sum_iJ_i^\top J_i$. Why can using every pixel from one strongly textured edge still produce a poorly conditioned $H$? How does the pixel-selection strategy of a direct sparse method address this?
questions.answer:
Neighbouring pixels on the same edge have nearly parallel image gradients and very similar pose Jacobians. Their outer products $J_i^\top J_i$ therefore add almost the **same rank-one information** many times. The number of residuals grows, but the missing motion directions remain weak; $H$ has a large eigenvalue in one direction and tiny eigenvalues in others, so it is ill-conditioned.
A direct sparse method keeps pixels with sufficient gradient but distributes them over the image and across different gradient orientations and depths. This removes highly correlated measurements, preserves the independent directions that determine the pose, improves the eigenvalue spread of $H$, and makes the windowed optimisation much cheaper without losing proportional information.
questions.extend: More pixels do not automatically mean more information. What matters is the rank and conditioning of the summed Jacobian outer products.

questions.q: Which statements about photometric error for 2D-2D geometry are correct?
questions.answer: **Correct: 1, 2 and 4.** With calibrated images, direct two-view alignment optimises pose and depth/inverse depth under brightness consistency. The objective is non-convex and sensitive to initialisation. Inverse depth gives a numerically better parametrisation, especially for distant points.

options.text: For calibrated RGB images, the unknowns in the photometric error are pixel depths and the relative camera pose.
Photometric error typically relies on brightness consistency.
Minimising photometric error is not sensitive to the initial parameter values.
Inverse-depth parametrisation can improve numerical stability.

questions.q: Which factors are mainly modelled by photometric calibration?
questions.answer: **Correct: response function, exposure time and vignetting.** Photometric calibration maps recorded intensity back toward scene irradiance by correcting the camera response, exposure and spatial attenuation. Rolling shutter is a geometric/time-readout effect and is handled by a motion/readout model rather than photometric calibration.

questions.q: For calibrated images, a direct relative-pose objective is $\min\sum_i\rho(I_1(p_i)-I_2(q_i))$. Express the reprojection $q_i$ using known $K$, known depth $d_i$ at $p_i$, and unknown $R,t$ from camera 1 to camera 2. What is $\rho$ and why is it used?
questions.answer:
Using homogeneous $p_i$, back-project and transform:
$$\hat p_i=K^{-1}p_i,\qquad P_i=d_i\hat p_i,\qquad Q_i=RP_i+t.$$
Project into image 2:
$$\tilde q_i=KQ_i,\qquad q_i=\pi(\tilde q_i),$$
where $\pi$ divides by the third homogeneous coordinate. $\rho$ is a **robust kernel**, such as Huber loss, which limits the influence of outlying photometric residuals.

knowledge_points.title: Pose Graph Optimisation and Loop Closure
knowledge_points.recap:
**Why.** Frame-to-frame tracking (visual odometry) accumulates **drift**: small errors compound over a long trajectory. Recognising that the camera has returned to a previously visited place — a **loop closure** — adds a constraint between two temporally distant frames and lets the accumulated error be redistributed over the whole loop, restoring **global consistency**.
**Pose graph.** Nodes are keyframe poses $T_i\in SE(3)$ (or $\operatorname{Sim}(3)$ in monocular SLAM, where the scale also drifts); edges are relative-pose measurements $\hat T_{ij}$ from tracking or from loop-closure detection. The residual of an edge is
$$r_{ij}=\log\big(\hat T_{ij}^{-1}\,T_i^{-1}T_j\big)^\vee\in\mathbb{R}^6,$$
i.e. the **error transformation** between the measured and the predicted relative pose, mapped into the Lie algebra so it can be used in a least-squares cost $\sum_{(i,j)}\|r_{ij}\|_{\Sigma_{ij}}^2$. It vanishes exactly when $T_i^{-1}T_j=\hat T_{ij}$.
**Dimension and sparsity.** With $N$ keyframes the problem has $6N$ unknowns (one twist per pose, minus a fixed gauge). Each edge couples exactly **two** poses, so the Hessian is block-sparse with $6\times6$ blocks: a pure chain of $N$ frames gives a **block-tridiagonal** Hessian ($N-1$ edges), and a single loop-closure constraint adds **one** off-diagonal block pair connecting the two ends — turning the chain into a cycle. The structure stays extremely sparse, which is why pose-graph optimisation scales to thousands of keyframes while full bundle adjustment does not.
**Loop-closure detection** typically uses **images** (bag-of-words place recognition on appearance) and **point clouds** (geometric registration), with a geometric verification step to reject false positives — a wrong loop closure is far more damaging than a missed one.
**Where it sits in a system.** SLAM $\approx$ visual odometry $+$ loop closure. LSD-SLAM tracks by direct $\mathfrak{sim}(3)$ image alignment and optimises a $\operatorname{Sim}(3)$ pose graph; DSO performs a **windowed joint optimisation** of poses, depths and photometric parameters, marginalising old frames out of the window.

questions.q: (a) What does the pose-graph residual $r_{ij}=\log\big(\hat T_{ij}^{-1}T_i^{-1}T_j\big)$ measure? (b) What is the dimension of the optimisation problem, and how does a loop-closure constraint change the graph? (c) For a chain of $N$ frames plus one loop-closure edge, describe the sparsity of the Hessian.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $T_i^{-1}T_j$ is the **predicted** relative pose from the current estimates, and $\hat T_{ij}$ is the **measured** one (from tracking or loop closure). Their composition $\hat T_{ij}^{-1}T_i^{-1}T_j$ is the residual *transformation*, which equals the identity when the estimate agrees with the measurement. Taking $\log$ maps it into $\mathfrak{se}(3)\cong\mathbb{R}^6$, giving a vector-valued residual that can be squared in a least-squares cost.
**(b)** With $N$ keyframes there are $6N$ unknowns — six twist coordinates per pose (one pose is fixed to remove the gauge freedom, leaving $6(N-1)$ effective). A loop closure adds **one extra edge** between two temporally distant nodes; it does not add unknowns, but it turns the open chain into a **cycle**, which is what allows the accumulated drift to be redistributed.
**(c)** Each edge couples exactly two poses, so the Hessian has a $6\times6$ block per pose pair that shares an edge. A chain of $N$ frames has $N-1$ consecutive edges, giving a **block-tridiagonal** Hessian. The single loop-closure edge adds **one** symmetric pair of off-diagonal blocks linking the first and last nodes — a "corner" entry that makes the matrix cyclic rather than banded. The overall density remains $O(N)$ non-zero blocks.
questions.extend: Because only the *relative* poses are measured, the absolute pose of the graph is unobservable — one node must be fixed, or the Hessian is singular by six dimensions.

questions.q: Explain the role of loop closure and pose-graph optimisation in a large-scale direct SLAM system such as LSD-SLAM, and why $\operatorname{Sim}(3)$ rather than $SE(3)$ is used in the monocular case.
questions.answer:
**Drift.** Tracking estimates each new frame relative to the previous one, so errors accumulate: after a long trajectory the map is locally accurate but globally inconsistent.
**Loop closure** detects that the camera has revisited a place and adds a constraint between two distant keyframes. Optimising the pose graph then spreads the accumulated error around the loop, restoring **global consistency** without re-optimising every pixel.
**Why $\operatorname{Sim}(3)$.** In **monocular** SLAM the absolute scale is unobservable, and it does not merely stay unknown — it **drifts** over the trajectory. So two keyframes can differ not only by a rigid motion but also by a scale factor. Optimising over $\operatorname{Sim}(3)$ (rotation, translation **and** scale, 7 DOF) lets the loop closure correct scale drift as well; LSD-SLAM's tracking is a direct $\mathfrak{sim}(3)$ image alignment for exactly this reason.
**Contrast with DSO,** which instead performs a **windowed joint optimisation** of poses, inverse depths and photometric parameters, marginalising older keyframes out of the sliding window rather than maintaining a global pose graph.

questions.q: A pose graph has residual $r_{ij}=\log(\hat T_{ij}^{-1}T_i^{-1}T_j)^\vee$. (a) Show when it is zero. (b) Explain the gauge freedom and one valid way to remove it. (c) Describe the Hessian block pattern for a chain of $N$ poses after adding one loop edge between poses $1$ and $N$.
questions.answer:
The logarithm is zero exactly when its argument is the identity, hence
$$T_i^{-1}T_j=\hat T_{ij}.$$
Left-multiplying every pose by the same global transform leaves all relative poses unchanged, so the graph has a global-pose gauge; fix one pose or add an equivalent prior. A chain produces a block-tridiagonal Hessian with $6\times6$ pose blocks. The loop edge adds one symmetric off-diagonal block pair coupling poses $1$ and $N$ and corresponding diagonal contributions, turning the chain into a sparse cycle rather than a dense system.
questions.extend: Cremers-style coverage question; not a past-paper citation.

questions.q: Why does monocular loop closure often optimize a $\operatorname{Sim}(3)$ pose graph instead of $SE(3)$? State the residual dimension, the additional state variable, and two defenses against a false loop-closure edge.
questions.answer: Monocular visual odometry can accumulate scale drift as well as rotational and translational drift. $SE(3)$ has no scale variable, whereas $\operatorname{Sim}(3)$ adds one log-scale parameter, giving a 7D tangent-space residual instead of a 6D one. A loop can then correct scale inconsistency around the cycle. False loops are dangerous global constraints; defenses include appearance retrieval followed by geometric verification, consistency with neighboring poses, robust losses or switchable constraints, and rejecting edges whose inlier count or reprojection residual is poor.
questions.extend: Cremers-style coverage question; not a past-paper citation.
